Name: einstellung_method_fixation
Title: Mental Set in Machines: An Einstellung Effect Where Prior Problems Fixate a Reasoning Model on a Costly Method and Blind It to Simpler Ones
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the classic Einstellung (mental-set) effect from cognitive psychology, we hypothesize that after a reasoning model solves a run of problems that all require the same method, it rigidly reapplies that method to a subsequent problem that admits a far simpler solution—spending more tokens and often failing to find the shortcut—even though it solves the same problem correctly and cheaply in isolation. This method-fixation is not driven by the target problem's difficulty but by a method-commitment representation carried over from the preceding context, which can be located and causally steered to release the fixation.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here. (1) Cognitive psychology: the Einstellung / water-jar effect (Luchins 1942) and expertise-induced fixation (Bilalić et al.) show that a repeated successful method creates a mental set that blocks discovery of simpler solutions—a robust, authoritative human finding. (2) Efficient-reasoning and reuse work: external memory/retrieval methods (Retrieval-of-Thought, Buffer of Thoughts, MemShare, ENGRAM-R, Graph-Memoized, InftyThink-with-memory) REUSE prior reasoning to speed up new problems, and interpretability work shows in-context task/method reuse via shared circuits (Circuit Component Reuse 2023) and reasoning-length priors set pre-generation (On Reasoning Strength Planning 2025). Crucially, all reuse work treats reuse as BENEFICIAL and studies helpful transfer; none studies HARMFUL over-reuse—rigidity that inflates compute and blinds the model to shortcuts. My prior 'analogical_transfer_gate' proposal studied FAILURE to transfer a helpful analog; this is the opposite failure: pathological SUCCESS of transfer that fixates the model. My 'reasoning_length_contagion' proposal concerned length carry-over but not method rigidity or shortcut-blindness. We are the first to (a) demonstrate an Einstellung effect in reasoning LLMs as joint compute-inflation + shortcut-blindness, (b) dissociate it from target difficulty, and (c) locate and causally steer a method-commitment representation that releases the set.
Abstract: Humans who repeatedly solve problems with one method develop a mental set that leads them to rigidly reapply it, missing simpler solutions—the Einstellung effect. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit this rigidity. We construct 'Einstellung sequences': a run of prime problems all solvable only by a costly method M, followed by a critical target problem that admits both M and a much simpler shortcut S, with a matched no-prime control that presents the same target in isolation. We hypothesize that primed models rigidly apply M to the target—spending more tokens and more often failing to use S—even though the target is identical, and that this fixation is driven not by the target's difficulty but by a method-commitment signal carried over from the prime context. Across arithmetic word problems, algebra, and combinatorics on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure shortcut-usage rate, reasoning-token count, and accuracy on the critical target as a function of prime length, using a mixed-effects decomposition to dissociate the prime effect from target difficulty. Mechanistically, we probe whether the prompt-boundary residual stream at the target encodes a method-commitment signal separable from a difficulty probe, localize it, causally validate via activation patching (patch a no-prime state into a primed context and observe shortcut recovery), and steer the signal to release the set. We test a training-free debiasing intervention that restores shortcut use and cuts tokens. Beyond a novel cognitive-transfer phenomenon, method-fixation is a deployment risk: in agentic and multi-turn settings, recent problem history can silently make models reason worse and more expensively.
Experiments: 1) Build Einstellung sequences: For each critical TARGET problem, hand-design (with templates + LLM/human verification) a shortcut S (a simple insight, e.g. a symmetry, a closed-form, a cancellation) and a costly-but-valid method M (e.g. brute-force enumeration, long algebraic derivation). Create PRIME problems that are ONLY solvable by M and NOT by S. Assemble sequences: N prime problems (N in {0,1,3,5}) then the target. N=0 is the no-prime control. Use classic-analog domains: water-jar-style arithmetic, algebra, and small combinatorics/counting. Verify targets are solvable by both S and M in isolation and that primes admit only M. 2) Establish the Einstellung effect (behavioral): Generate reasoning traces on the target after each prime length. Metrics on the critical target: (i) shortcut-usage rate (did the trace employ S? via step-template matching + LLM-judge), (ii) reasoning-token count, (iii) accuracy. Hypothesis: as prime length grows, shortcut usage drops, tokens rise, and accuracy on shortcut-favoring targets falls, relative to N=0. Report within-target effect sizes and dose-response over N. Include a 'diverse-prime' control (primes solved by varied methods) to show fixation requires METHOD-repetition, not mere context length. 3) Dissociation from difficulty: Mixed-effects model of shortcut-usage / tokens / accuracy with random effect for target identity (intrinsic difficulty) and fixed effect for prime length; test for a significant prime effect after accounting for target identity; control raw prompt length with a covariate and a length-matched irrelevant-filler prime. 4) Wasted vs genuine compute: Truncate-and-resume to estimate minimal-solve length via S; test whether priming inflates tokens beyond the S-minimal solve (rigid M execution) rather than adding needed reasoning. 5) Location — method-commitment probe: At the target's prompt boundary (last token before any target reasoning token), extract residual-stream activations; train a linear probe to predict whether the model will use S vs M on the target, and a classifier for prime-method identity. Test whether, for identical targets, the probe's prediction shifts with prime length. Compare to a target-difficulty probe (trained on isolated pass-rate); test separability via principal angles between the method-commitment direction and the difficulty direction and via joint-model predictive gain. Layer sweep to localize. 6) Causal validation — patching: Patch the prompt-boundary residual state from a no-prime (S-inducing) context into the matched primed context (same target) and measure whether the model recovers the shortcut (S-usage up, tokens down). Controls: matched-random-direction patch, off-target accuracy preserved; report sign, dose, specificity. Reverse: patch primed state into no-prime context to induce fixation. 7) Causal intervention — releasing the set (debiasing): Derive a method-commitment steering direction (difference-of-means between primed and no-prime boundary states) and steer primed targets to release fixation. Metrics: shortcut-usage recovery, tokens-at-equal-accuracy, accuracy gain on shortcut-favoring targets; compare to a simple prompt-based fix ('consider whether a simpler method applies'). Verify a matched-random direction does not release the set (specificity). 8) Modulators & generalization: vary prime-method salience, insert an explicit 'fresh problem' delimiter (does it reset the set?), and test cross-domain fixation. Transfer probe/steering across datasets and model scales without retraining; test whether RL-tuned models fixate more or less.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Constructing targets with a clean shortcut S and a genuinely-only-M prime set is nontrivial; we mitigate with templated generation plus human/LLM verification that primes exclude S and targets admit both, and treat ambiguous items separately. The effect could be confounded by context length rather than method-repetition; the diverse-prime control, length-matched filler prime, and mixed-effects analysis isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result refuting the transfer. Shortcut-usage detection (step-template + LLM-judge) is noisy; we validate with human spot-checks and report agreement. The method-commitment signal may be inseparable from a generic difficulty/uncertainty direction; the separability analysis, patching, and difficulty-probe comparison address this, and overlap with an in-context task-vector direction would itself be an interesting mechanistic finding. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included, and releasing the set could over-trigger on problems where M is genuinely required (specificity check on M-only targets). The effect may be small in strongly instruction-tuned models trained to treat each problem freshly (a valuable boundary condition) and may be model-family and scale specific. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.
